To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the spontaneously hypertensive rats made normotensive with treatment show a pattern of renal lesions and proteinuria similar to that of the hypertensive rats, suggesting that the renal lesions of SHR are a consequence of the genetic defect of the vascular system of SHR, and not of the hypertension.

the spontaneously hypertensive (SHR) rat develops glomerular lesions and proteinuria at normal blood pressure, and that the lesions are identical to those found in SHR's at high blood pressure, except for a delay in their appearance.

The spontaneously hypertensive rat (SHR) has a genetically determined defect in the vascular wall that is strongly associated with the hypertension and is responsible for the arteriolar sclerosis that develops in this strain.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the pathogenesis of hypertension, particularly in its relationship to arteriolar and glomerular lesions.
the study of the relationship of hypertension to renal lesions and proteinuria, and with the effects of treatment on the development and course of these lesions in the SHR.
the pathogenesis of the hypertensive vascular disease and its relation to the genetic basis for hypertension in the rat.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the renal lesions in normotension are not a direct result of hypertension, but rather a result of an intrinsic vascular defect that is strongly associated with the genetic defect that causes hypertension.
hypertension in the SHR is a primary disease of the vascular wall, and not of the heart, kidney, or brain.
the SHR has a genetically determined vascular defect which, when combined with the hypertension, leads to glomerular and vascular damage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
hypertension and proteinuria in SHR are not causally related, and that hypertension is a secondary phenomenon to the renal lesions and proteinuria.
the SHR's are genetically abnormal in the sense of having a defect in vascular integrity that is strongly associated with the development of hypertension.

SHR's have an inherent tendency for the development of arteriosclerosis which is not related to the hypertensive process, but which may be related to the genetic defect in the membrane structure of vascular cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that

treatment of hypertension in SHR's can prevent the development of renal lesions and proteinuria, and thus prolong life, but the renal lesions and protein excretion are not a consequence of the hypertension.
hypertension is a risk factor in the development of renal disease.
the SHR's vascular defect is a major factor in the development of renal disease and proteinuria in this animal.
